subject: Code for Poisson Hurdle Model in Documentation Is Slow

messages.author: d24e3e0d2299ccfd
messages.subject: Code for Poisson Hurdle Model in Documentation Is Slow
parts:
Note that the code provided for the Poisson Hurdle Model on p. 108 is too slow to run on medium-sized datasets. I was using a randomly generated dataset of 10000 points.

The documentation suggests the following code:
  data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> y[N];
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
    real<lower=0> lambda;
  }
  model {
    for (n in 1:N) {
      (y[n] == 0) ~ bernoulli(theta);
      if (y[n] > 0)
        y[n] ~ poisson(lambda) T[1,];
    }
  }

But it's a lot faster if we code things using increment_log_prob as follows:

  data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> y[N];
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
    real<lower=0> lambda;
  }
  model {
    for (n in 1:N) {
      if (y[n] == 0)
        increment_log_prob(
            bernoulli_log(1, theta));
      else
        increment_log_prob(
            bernoulli_log(0, theta) +
            poisson_log(y[n], lambda) -
            log(1 - exp(-lambda)));
    }
  }

Should the documentation be updated to inform the users of this?

I actually don't see that. What I do see is that there is a difference between the first and subsequent runs given the same model, and the inc_log_prob model is actually the slowest, at least using 1 iteration on my machine. Here are three versions of roughly the identical model. The first two models are what you bring above, and the last uses poisson_log.

P1.stan

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> y[N];
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
    real<lower=0> lambda;
  }
  model {
    for (n in 1:N) {
      (y[n] == 0) ~ bernoulli(theta);
      if (y[n] > 0)
        y[n] ~ poisson(lambda) T[1,];
    }
  }
P2.stan

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> y[N];
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
    real<lower=0> lambda;
  }
  model {
    for (n in 1:N) {
      if (y[n] == 0)
        increment_log_prob(
            bernoulli_log(1, theta));
      else
        increment_log_prob(
            bernoulli_log(0, theta) +
            poisson_log(y[n], lambda) -
            log(1 - exp(-lambda)));
    }
  }
P3.stan

data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> y[N];
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
real alpha;

}

    for (n in 1:N) {

      if (y[n] > 0)

y[n] ~ poisson_log(alpha);

parts: On Tuesday, August 4, 2015 at 4:41:45 PM UTC-4, Avraham Adler wrote:

P3.stan
  data {
    int<lower=0> N;
    int<lower=0> y[N];
  }
  parameters {
    real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
    real alpha;
  }
  model {
    for (n in 1:N) {
      (y[n] == 0) ~ bernoulli(theta);
      if (y[n] > 0)
        y[n] ~ poisson_log(alpha);
    }
  }
  generated quantities{
    real<lower = 0> lambda;
      lambda <- exp(alpha);
 }
The models results are pretty much identical, and it is educational that P3 is the quickest, even though it has the extra step of exponentiating lambda in the generated quantities block.

You can make this model go faster for large N by passing in the data appropriately and avoiding 2N sampling statements

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0,upper=1> is_zero[N];
  int<lower=1> y[N - sum(is_zero)];
}
parameters {
  real logit_theta;
  real log_alpha;
}
model {
  is_zero ~ bernoulli_logit(logit_theta);
  y ~ poisson_log(log_alpha);
}
generated quantities {
  real theta;
  real alpha;
  theta <- inv_logit(logit_theta);
  alpha <- exp(log_alpha);
}

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Code for Poisson Hurdle Model in Documentation Is Slow
parts:
We're torn between pedagogy and efficiency. Andrew wants us
to write the most efficient models possible, but then they get
confusing.

I'd think we could go one step further and keep the data as is,
calculate the sufficient stats in Stan, and convert the Bernoullis
to a single binomial.


functions {
int num_non_zeros(int[] y) {
int tot;
tot <- 0;
for (i in 1:size(y))
tot <- tot + (y[i] > 0);
return tot;
}
int[] non_zero_ys(int[] y) {
int[num_non_zeros(y)] nz_ys;
int pos;
pos <- 1;
for (i in 1:size(y)) {
if (y[i] > 0) {
nz_ys[pos] <- y[i];
pos <- pos + 1;
}
}
return nz_ys;

}
}
data {
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> y[N];
}

transformed data {
int sum_y;
int size_y;
int<lower=1> non_zero_ys[num_non_zeros(y)]

sum_y <- sum(y);
size_y <- size(y);
non_zero_ys <- non_zero(ys);
}
parameters {
real<lower=0, upper=1> one_minus_theta;
real alpha;
}
model {
sum_y ~ binomial(size_y, one_minus_theta);
non_zero_ys ~ poisson(alpha);
}
generated quantities {
real<lower=0, upper=1> theta;
theta <- 1 - one_minus_theta;
}

And you won't be able to save that 1 - theta operation each
time if the prior on theta doesn't satisfy
p(theta) == p(1 - theta)) as the implicit uniform prior does.

I haven't tried to run this by the way, so indices and things
may be off, but I'm pretty sure the basic idea's right.

- Bob

parts: Why doesn't the model P3.stan require a truncation statement T[1,]?  The poisson_log function gives the raw Poisson PDF - it needs to be deflated by 1 - exp(-lambda) = 1-exp(-exp(alpha)).  Are you making the approximation here that this is equal to 1?  This is valid for moderately sized samples, but not where there are small numbers of counts.
